UA-63.name: Kharkiv Oblast
UA-63.overview: The forest-steppe and steppe of today's Kharkiv Oblast, drained by the Siverskyi Donets and Oskil rivers, was a frontier between farming and nomadic peoples for millennia, from Bronze Age herders and Scythian-era hillforts to the Khazar-era Saltovo-Mayaki culture. Long part of the depopulated Wild Fields, it was resettled from the 1630s-1650s by Ukrainian Cossacks and peasants under Muscovite protection, becoming the core of Sloboda Ukraine with Kharkiv founded around 1654. In the 19th and 20th centuries Kharkiv grew into a university, industrial and tank-building centre and was the capital of Soviet Ukraine from 1919 to 1934; the region suffered the Holodomor and four battles of World War II. Since 2022 it has been a front-line region: the north and east were occupied in 2022 and largely liberated that September, while Russia's 2024 northern offensive and the long fight for Kupiansk kept parts of the oblast contested into 2026.

trypillia.control: Neolithic-Eneolithic hunter-fisher and early herding communities
trypillia.summary: The Trypillia farming culture did not reach this far east. The Donets valley was home to Dnieper-Donets culture communities with comb-decorated pottery, and the Sredny Stog culture, an early horse-using steppe culture, reached the southern parts of the area.

bronze-age-steppe.summary: Burial mounds (kurgans) of the Yamnaya, Catacomb and Srubna cultures dot the steppe south of the Donets. Towards the end of the Bronze Age the forest-steppe north of the Donets belonged to the Bondarikha culture, named after a site in this oblast.

cimmerians.control: Late Bondarikha forest-steppe farmers; Cimmerian-era nomads on the steppe
cimmerians.summary: Late Bondarikha settlements continued in the Donets and Oskil valleys, while steppe nomads of the Cimmerian period ranged to the south. Iron began to replace bronze for tools and weapons.

scythians.control: Scythian-era forest-steppe farmers (Siverskyi Donets group); nomadic Scythians to the south
scythians.summary: The forest-steppe of the upper Donets, Udy and Merla rivers had a dense network of Scythian-era farming settlements and hillforts, a local group of the forest-steppe Scythian culture. The giant Bilsk hillfort, often identified with Herodotus's Gelonus, lay just west of today's oblast border in Poltava Oblast.
scythians.military: Earthwork hillforts such as those near Liubotyn and on the Donets guarded the farming communities against steppe raids.

sarmatians.summary: Sarmatians from the east displaced the Scythians and pushed into the forest-steppe; Sarmatian kurgan burials are found along the Donets and Oskil. Settled farming declined in the area.

goths-chernyakhov.summary: The Kharkiv region formed the eastern edge of the Chernyakhov culture, with farming villages, wheel-made pottery and Roman imports along the Udy and Donets. The population mixed Slavic, Gothic and Sarmatian elements.

huns.control: Hunnic domination; Kyiv-culture communities in the north
huns.summary: The Hunnic invasion of the 370s ended the Chernyakhov culture here. Small Kiev-culture settlements, usually linked with early Slavs or Balts, survived in the northern forest-steppe.

antes.control: Early Slavic (Penkovka culture, Antes) settlers; Bulgar and Avar nomads
antes.summary: Penkovka-culture villages, attributed to the Antes, spread along the rivers of the forest-steppe, while Kutrigur and Avar nomads controlled the steppe to the south.

east-slavic-tribes.control: Khazar Khaganate (Saltovo-Mayaki culture); Severians in the north-west
east-slavic-tribes.summary: The Donets valley became a heartland of the Khazar-era Saltovo-Mayaki culture, named in part after Verkhnii Saltiv in this oblast, with Alan and Bulgar populations, white-stone hillforts and large catacomb cemeteries. Slavic Severians settled the north-west and paid tribute to the Khazars.
east-slavic-tribes.military: Khazar-era white-stone fortresses such as Verkhnii Saltiv guarded the Donets trade route.

kyivan-rus-formation.control: Khazar sphere, then Pecheneg steppe after 965
kyivan-rus-formation.summary: Saltovo-Mayaki settlements declined as Pechenegs moved in and as Sviatoslav of Kyiv destroyed Khazar power in 965. The Severian lands to the north-west came under Kyiv's rule.

kyivan-rus-volodymyr.control: Rus' frontier (Severian lands) and Pecheneg steppe
kyivan-rus-volodymyr.summary: The area lay beyond Volodymyr's southern defensive lines, a thinly settled borderland between Rus' Severian settlements and Pecheneg pastures.

kyivan-rus-peak.control: Chernihiv lands (north-west fringe); Pecheneg and Tork steppe
kyivan-rus-peak.summary: The north-west fringe belonged to the left-bank lands ruled from Chernihiv after 1024; the rest was steppe passing from Pechenegs to Torks.

rus-fragmentation.summary: Cumans dominated the Donets steppe. The Rus' frontier town of Donets, at the hillfort near today's Kharkiv, is mentioned in the Tale of Igor's Campaign as the place Prince Igor reached after escaping Cuman captivity in 1185.
rus-fragmentation.military: Igor Sviatoslavich's 1185 campaign against the Cumans marched along the Donets; Rus'-Cuman wars were fought across the area.

galicia-volhynia.control: Cuman steppe, conquered by the Mongols 1239-1240
galicia-volhynia.summary: The area lay far east of Galicia-Volhynia in Cuman lands. The Mongol campaigns of 1239-1240 destroyed the remaining Rus' frontier settlements and dispersed the Cumans.

mongol-period.summary: The area became nomadic pasture of the Golden Horde and was largely depopulated, the start of its history as part of the Wild Fields.

lithuania-poland.control: Wild Fields; nominal Lithuanian and later Muscovite frontier, Crimean Tatar raiding zone
lithuania-poland.summary: The almost empty steppe was crossed by the Muravsky Trail, the main Crimean Tatar raiding route towards Muscovy. Muscovite frontier patrols and Cossack fishermen and hunters were the only regular visitors.
lithuania-poland.military: Muscovy organised guard and patrol posts (storozhi) along the Donets to watch the Tatar trails.

commonwealth.summary: In 1638 Cossacks led by Yakiv Ostryanyn, fleeing the failed uprising against Poland, founded a settlement at Chuhuiv under Muscovite protection, an early step in the Ukrainian resettlement of the region.
commonwealth.military: Muscovy built fortified towns and the Belgorod defensive line just to the north in the 1630s-1650s to block Tatar raids.

cossack-hetmanate.summary: Fleeing war on the Right Bank, Ukrainian settlers founded Kharkiv around 1654 along with other free settlements (slobody), keeping Cossack self-government under the tsar. This was the birth of Sloboda Ukraine.
cossack-hetmanate.military: Kharkiv was built as a wooden fortress; the settlers formed a Cossack regiment that defended the frontier against Tatar raids.

the-ruin.summary: Refugees from the Ruin swelled the population. The area was organised into Sloboda Cossack regiments, including the Kharkiv and Izium regiments, under Muscovite governors.
the-ruin.military: The Kharkiv and Izium Sloboda regiments fought Tatar raids and served in Muscovite campaigns, including the Chyhyryn and Crimean campaigns; the Izium fortified line was built about 1679-1681.

hetmanate-decline.control: Russian Empire (Sloboda regiments until 1765, then Sloboda Ukraine Governorate)
hetmanate-decline.summary: The Kharkiv Collegium (1726) made Kharkiv an educational centre, and the philosopher Hryhorii Skovoroda taught there. In 1765 Catherine II abolished the Sloboda Cossack regiments and created the Sloboda Ukraine Governorate.
hetmanate-decline.military: The Ukrainian Line of forts (1731-1742) was built across the south of the oblast against the Crimean Tatars; the Sloboda regiments were turned into regular hussar regiments in 1765.

links.title: Abolition of the Cossack system in Sloboda Ukraine

partitions-crimea.summary: Kharkiv became the seat of a viceroyalty in 1780. The removal of the Tatar threat after 1783 allowed farming to spread south. Skovoroda died in 1794 at Pan-Ivanivka, now Skovorodynivka.

two-empires.control: Russian Empire (Sloboda Ukraine, from 1835 Kharkov Governorate)
two-empires.summary: Kharkiv University, founded in 1805 on Vasily Karazin's initiative, made the city the first centre of modern Ukrainian scholarship and literature; Hryhorii Kvitka-Osnovianenko wrote the first Ukrainian prose there. Large fairs made Kharkiv a trading hub.
two-empires.military: Arakcheyev's military settlements were set up around Chuhuiv; their brutal regime provoked the Chuhuiv uprising of 1819.

links.title: V. N. Karazin Kharkiv National University

national-revival.summary: Railways from 1869 and the Kharkiv Locomotive Factory (1895) turned Kharkiv into a major industrial city. It was also a political centre: the Revolutionary Ukrainian Party was founded there in 1900 and Mykola Mikhnovsky published Samostiina Ukraina, an early call for full independence.

ukrainian-revolution.control: Contested: Bolshevik Soviet Ukraine, then UNR and Hetmanate under German occupation
ukrainian-revolution.summary: In December 1917 the Bolsheviks proclaimed the Ukrainian People's Republic of Soviets in Kharkiv as a rival to the Kyiv Central Rada, and in February 1918 the Donetsk-Krivoy Rog Soviet Republic was declared there. German troops took the city in April 1918 and the area was part of Skoropadsky's Hetmanate until late 1918.
ukrainian-revolution.military: Red Guards under Antonov-Ovseenko used Kharkiv as the base for the first Bolshevik invasion of Ukraine (December 1917 to January 1918).

soviet-takeover.summary: The Red Army took Kharkiv in January 1919 and made it the capital of the Ukrainian SSR. Denikin's Volunteer Army held the region from June to December 1919, after which Soviet rule was restored.
soviet-takeover.military: Denikin's Volunteer Army captured Kharkiv in June 1919 during its march on Moscow; the Red Army retook it in December 1919.

soviet-ukraine-1920s.summary: As the Soviet Ukrainian capital, Kharkiv was the centre of Ukrainization and of a cultural renaissance led by writers such as Mykola Khvylovy. Constructivist landmarks such as Derzhprom (1925-1928) and the Slovo writers' building were built, and the Kharkiv Tractor Plant opened in 1931.

holodomor-terror.summary: Kharkiv Oblast, then much larger, had some of the highest Holodomor death rates in 1932-1933. Khvylovy shot himself in 1933 and many residents of the Slovo building were arrested or shot in the Executed Renaissance; the capital moved to Kyiv in 1934.

soviet-annexations.summary: In spring 1940 the NKVD shot about 3,800 Polish prisoners of war from the Starobilsk camp in Kharkiv as part of the Katyn massacre and buried them in the Piatykhatky forest. The T-34 tank was designed by Mikhail Koshkin's bureau at Kharkiv's Factory No. 183.
soviet-annexations.military: Kharkiv's Factory No. 183 began series production of the T-34 in 1940.

nazi-occupation.control: Nazi German military occupation (October 1941 to August 1943)
nazi-occupation.summary: Kharkiv fell on 24 October 1941 after its factories were evacuated east. About 15,000 Jews were murdered at Drobytsky Yar in the winter of 1941-1942, and thousands of residents starved under occupation.
nazi-occupation.military: The city changed hands four times: the First Battle of Kharkov (October 1941), the failed Soviet offensive of May 1942 near Barvinkove, the Soviet recapture and German counterattack of February-March 1943, and final liberation on 23 August 1943 in the Belgorod-Kharkov offensive.

postwar-ussr.summary: Kharkiv was rebuilt from heavy war damage while the countryside suffered the famine of 1946-1947. The Malyshev tank factory and aircraft and tractor plants made the city a core of Soviet defence industry.
postwar-ussr.military: The Malyshev factory (formerly No. 183) returned from the Urals and resumed tank design and production.

soviet-ukraine-late.summary: Kharkiv grew to about 1.5 million people, a centre of engineering, physics (the Kharkiv Institute of Physics and Technology) and higher education, and opened Ukraine's second metro in 1975. Public life was heavily Russified.
soviet-ukraine-late.military: Kharkiv factories built tanks such as the T-64 and T-80UD, and the Kharkiv Guards tank school trained officers.

links.title: Kharkiv Institute of Physics and Technology

independence.summary: In the December 1991 referendum about 86% of voters in the oblast backed independence. Defence plants declined, while trade such as the huge Barabashovo market and the universities sustained the city.

orange-to-euromaidan.summary: The region leaned towards Viktor Yanukovych's Party of Regions, led locally by Mykhailo Dobkin and Hennadiy Kernes. The 2010 Kharkiv Pact extended Russia's Black Sea Fleet lease in Crimea, and Kharkiv hosted Euro 2012 matches.

crimea-donbas-war.control: Ukraine (rear area of the Donbas front)
crimea-donbas-war.summary: Pro-Russian activists stormed the regional administration in March-April 2014 and proclaimed a 'Kharkiv People's Republic', but Interior Ministry forces cleared the building on 8 April and the separatist movement collapsed. Kharkiv became a major military, medical and refugee hub for the Donbas war.
crimea-donbas-war.military: Kharkiv was a logistics base for the Anti-Terrorist Operation; a bombing of a unity march killed four people in February 2015, and the Balakliia ammunition depot exploded in March 2017, probably due to sabotage.

full-scale-invasion.control: Contested: north and east occupied February-September 2022, then mostly liberated
full-scale-invasion.summary: On 24 February 2022 Russian forces crossed the border, besieged Kharkiv city and occupied Kupiansk, Vovchansk, Balakliia and, on 1 April, Izium. The September 2022 Kharkiv counteroffensive liberated about 12,000 km², including Balakliia, Izium and Kupiansk, and revealed mass graves and torture sites in Izium.
full-scale-invasion.military: Ukraine held Kharkiv city in heavy street fighting and pushed Russian troops back toward the border in May 2022; the surprise September offensive collapsed Russia's front east to the Oskil river, leaving only a small strip east of the Oskil occupied.

war-of-attrition.control: Mostly Ukraine; Russian-held border strips and areas east of the Oskil
war-of-attrition.summary: Russian forces pressed on Kupiansk and the Oskil front from late 2023, and on 10 May 2024 launched a new cross-border offensive in the north, reaching Vovchansk and Lyptsi before stalling. Kharkiv city came under constant glide-bomb and missile strikes, and a strike on a café in Hroza in October 2023 killed 59 people.
war-of-attrition.military: The 2024 northern offensive turned Vovchansk into a ruined front-line town; by late 2024 Russian troops reached the Oskil near Kupiansk and took bridgeheads on its west bank.

war-2025-2026.control: Mostly Ukraine; Russian-held strips along the border, around Vovchansk and east of the Oskil; Kupiansk contested
war-2025-2026.summary: Russian infiltration groups entered Kupiansk in mid-2025 and Russia claimed its capture on 20 November 2025, but Ukrainian counterattacks cleared much of the city by December 2025; through 2026 control of the town has remained disputed. Russia's capture of Vovchansk in late 2025 was at least partly confirmed. Kharkiv city continued to face frequent drone and missile strikes.
war-2025-2026.military: In autumn 2026 ISW assessed net Russian losses of territory around Kupiansk, and Ukrainian forces claimed an operation through underground pipelines behind Russian lines in October 2026; these claims are not independently confirmed. Fighting also continued around Borova and on the Oskil bridgeheads, and the exact front line is uncertain.

sources.title: ISW Russian Offensive Campaign Assessment, 20 October 2026

UA-09.name: Luhansk Oblast
UA-09.overview: Ukraine's easternmost oblast spans the steppe of the Siverskyi Donets valley and the Donets Ridge. After millennia as nomad pasture, from Bronze Age herders to Cumans and the Golden Horde, it was the empty Wild Fields until Sloboda Cossack, Don Cossack, Serbian military and peasant colonists settled it in the 17th and 18th centuries; Luhansk grew from a state foundry founded in 1795. Coal mining and heavy industry made it part of the Donbas, with a mixed Ukrainian and Russian population. Russian-backed forces seized the south in 2014 as the 'Luhansk People's Republic', and after the 2022 invasion Russia occupied almost the entire oblast, which it claims to have annexed; this is not recognized internationally.

trypillia.summary: Trypillian farmers never reached the Donets. Its valley was home to Dnieper-Donets culture communities and later to early steppe herders of the Sredny Stog horizon.

bronze-age-steppe.summary: Thousands of Bronze Age kurgans cover the area. Srubna-culture miners worked copper ores of the Donets Ridge, notably at Kartamysh near Popasna, one of the largest ancient mining centres in eastern Europe.

cimmerians.summary: Nomadic herders of the Cimmerian period used the Donets steppe; settlement traces are sparse.

scythians.control: Scythian nomads; Sauromatians beyond the Don
scythians.summary: The area lay on the eastern fringe of Scythia, bordering the Sauromatians beyond the Don. Scythian kurgans are found along the Donets and its tributaries.

sarmatians.summary: Sarmatian tribes, arriving from the Volga-Don steppe, took the area early; the Greek city of Tanais at the Don mouth traded with them.

goths-chernyakhov.control: Alans and Sarmatians; Gothic sphere to the west
goths-chernyakhov.summary: The steppe remained largely in the hands of Alan and Sarmatian nomads, at the eastern margin of the Gothic-dominated Chernyakhov zone.

huns.summary: The Huns crossed the Don around 370 and swept through these steppes on their way west.

antes.summary: Utigur and Kutrigur Bulgars and then the Avars and Turkic khaganate ranged over the area; by the 630s it lay within Old Great Bulgaria.

east-slavic-tribes.summary: Alan and Bulgar communities of the Saltovo-Mayaki culture farmed and herded along the Donets and Aidar under Khazar rule.
east-slavic-tribes.military: Khazar-era hillforts protected the Donets valley route.

kyivan-rus-formation.summary: Pechenegs entered the steppe around 900, and the Saltovo settlements declined after Sviatoslav's defeat of Khazaria in 965.

kyivan-rus-volodymyr.summary: The area was Pecheneg pasture far beyond the frontier of Volodymyr's Rus'.

kyivan-rus-peak.summary: Torks replaced the Pechenegs in the steppe around the mid-11th century, soon followed by the Cumans.

rus-fragmentation.summary: The Donets steppe was a core area of the Cumans, who left many carved stone statues (kurgan stelae) here. Prince Igor's army was destroyed in 1185 on the Kayala river, which many historians place in today's Luhansk or Donetsk region, though the site is disputed.
rus-fragmentation.military: Rus' princes campaigned deep into the Cuman steppe in 1111 (Sviatopolk and Volodymyr Monomakh) and 1185 (Igor Sviatoslavich).

galicia-volhynia.control: Cuman steppe, conquered by the Mongols
galicia-volhynia.summary: After the Rus'-Cuman defeat on the Kalka in 1223, the Mongols conquered these steppes in 1237-1240.

mongol-period.summary: The area was Golden Horde pasture; settled life almost disappeared.

lithuania-poland.control: Wild Fields (Crimean Tatar and Nogai pasture)
lithuania-poland.summary: The empty steppe was crossed by Tatar raiders; Don Cossacks began to appear along the lower Donets in the 16th century.

commonwealth.control: Wild Fields; Don Cossack and Muscovite frontier
commonwealth.summary: Don Cossack hunters and fishermen used the Donets and Aidar valleys; there were still almost no permanent settlements.

cossack-hetmanate.summary: Don Cossack outposts appeared on the Donets, among them the predecessor of Stanytsia Luhanska; the north began to receive Sloboda Ukrainian settlers.

the-ruin.summary: Ukrainian settlers founded slobody along the Aidar and Krasna rivers in the north, under the Ostrogozhsk and Izium Sloboda regiments. The Don Cossack Bulavin Rebellion of 1707-1708 spread through the Donets and Aidar settlements and was crushed by Peter I.
the-ruin.military: Peter I's punitive troops burned rebel Cossack towns along the Aidar and Donets in 1708.

hetmanate-decline.control: Russian Empire (Slavo-Serbia, Sloboda Ukraine, Don Host)
hetmanate-decline.summary: In 1753 the government created Slavo-Serbia between the Donets and the Luhan river for Serbian and other Balkan military colonists, founding settlements such as Slovianoserbsk.
hetmanate-decline.military: Slavo-Serbian hussar regiments guarded the frontier against the Crimean Khanate.

partitions-crimea.summary: In 1795 the Scottish engineer Charles Gascoigne founded the Luhansk state foundry to cast cannon for the Black Sea Fleet using local coal and iron; the workers' settlement grew into Luhansk.
partitions-crimea.military: The Luhansk foundry produced artillery and shot for the Black Sea Fleet.

two-empires.control: Russian Empire (Yekaterinoslav and Kharkov governorates, Don Host Oblast)
two-empires.summary: Coal mining began around Lysychansk, among the first in the Donbas. The lexicographer Vladimir Dal was born in Luhansk in 1801 and wrote as 'Kazak Luhansky'.

national-revival.summary: Railways and the coal boom drew workers from Russia and Ukraine into mining towns such as Kadiivka and Alchevsk; Luhansk gained the Hartmann locomotive works in 1896 and the Alchevsk steelworks opened in 1896. The rural north stayed Ukrainian-speaking.

ukrainian-revolution.control: Contested: Bolsheviks, UNR and Hetmanate with German forces, Don Cossack Whites
ukrainian-revolution.summary: Luhansk was part of the Bolshevik Donetsk-Krivoy Rog Soviet Republic in early 1918 until German and Ukrainian troops arrived in spring 1918. The local Bolshevik Kliment Voroshilov led a Red detachment from Luhansk to Tsaritsyn.
ukrainian-revolution.military: Voroshilov's 'Luhansk socialist detachment' fought German forces and then retreated east in April 1918.

soviet-takeover.control: Contested by Reds and Whites; Soviet from 1920
soviet-takeover.summary: The mining district changed hands repeatedly between Denikin's forces and the Red Army in 1919. In 1920 it became part of the Donets Governorate of the Ukrainian SSR.
soviet-takeover.military: Don Cossack and Volunteer Army units held the Donbas in the first half of 1919 before the Red Army retook it.

soviet-ukraine-1920s.summary: Mines and factories were rebuilt and expanded under the first five-year plan; the countryside was collectivized from 1929.

holodomor-terror.summary: Villages in the north starved in 1932-1933 while mining towns were partly protected by rations. In 1935 the miner Alexei Stakhanov's record shift in Kadiivka launched the Stakhanovite movement, Luhansk was renamed Voroshylovhrad, and in 1938 a separate oblast was created.

soviet-annexations.summary: The NKVD camp at Starobilsk held about 3,900 Polish officers captured in 1939; in spring 1940 they were shot in Kharkiv as part of the Katyn massacre.

nazi-occupation.summary: German and Italian troops occupied the oblast in July 1942. In Krasnodon (now Sorokyne) the Young Guard youth resistance group was destroyed in January 1943; Voroshylovhrad was liberated on 14 February 1943.
nazi-occupation.military: The Italian 8th Army held part of the front here before the Soviet winter offensive of 1942-1943.

postwar-ussr.summary: Mines and plants were rebuilt, partly with forced labour, and migration from Russia increased the Russian-speaking share of the population.

soviet-ukraine-late.summary: The city was called Luhansk again in 1958-1970 and Voroshylovhrad until 1990; Luhanskteplovoz built diesel locomotives for the whole USSR, and the chemical town of Sievierodonetsk grew from the 1930s-1950s. Donbas miners struck in 1989, helping to weaken Soviet authority.
soviet-ukraine-late.military: Voroshylovhrad hosted a military aviation school for navigators.

independence.summary: About 84% of voters supported independence in 1991, but the collapse of subsidised coal mining brought strikes, wage arrears and population decline.

orange-to-euromaidan.summary: In November 2004, during the Orange Revolution, regional officials met in Sievierodonetsk and threatened autonomy for the south-east. The Party of Regions dominated local politics until 2014.

crimea-donbas-war.control: Split: Russian-backed 'Luhansk People's Republic' in the south, Ukraine in the north
crimea-donbas-war.summary: Armed separatists seized the SBU building in Luhansk in April 2014 and proclaimed the 'Luhansk People's Republic' on 27 April. By late summer 2014, with Russian military help, it held Luhansk, Alchevsk, Kadiivka and the border; Ukraine held the north and moved the regional capital to Sievierodonetsk. The Minsk agreements froze the line along the Donets until 2022.
crimea-donbas-war.military: Battles included the siege of the Luhansk border base (June 2014), the shooting down of a Ukrainian Il-76 at Luhansk airport (14 June 2014, 49 killed), the fall of the airport in September 2014 and the fighting at Shchastia; volunteer units such as the Aidar Battalion fought here.

links.title: Siege of the Luhansk border base
2014 Ukrainian Air Force Ilyushin Il-76 shootdown

full-scale-invasion.summary: Russian forces quickly took Starobilsk, Shchastia and the north, then after weeks of fighting captured Rubizhne, Popasna (May), Sievierodonetsk (25 June) and Lysychansk (3 July 2022). In September 2022 Russia claimed to annex the oblast, which is not recognized internationally.
full-scale-invasion.military: Ukraine destroyed a Russian battalion crossing the Siverskyi Donets near Bilohorivka in May 2022; after the Kharkiv counteroffensive Ukrainian troops returned to the oblast's western edge near Svatove and Kreminna in autumn 2022.

war-of-attrition.control: Russian-occupied except a narrow western fringe held by Ukraine
war-of-attrition.summary: The front ran along the Svatove-Kreminna line, with prolonged fighting in the Serebrianka forest near Kreminna and around Bilohorivka. In the occupied areas Russia imposed its passports, curriculum and conscription and redeveloped Luhansk as a rear military hub.
war-of-attrition.military: Ukrainian brigades held small footholds around Bilohorivka, Nevske and villages on the Kharkiv border; Ukrainian long-range strikes hit depots and airfields in occupied Luhansk.

war-2025-2026.control: Russian-occupied; at most a few small border areas contested
war-2025-2026.summary: Russian forces took most of Bilohorivka by mid-2025, leaving Ukraine at most a small strip on the Kharkiv border, and Russian-installed officials claimed full control of the oblast in 2025. Ukraine's 3rd Assault Brigade retook the border village of Nadiia in March 2025. Whether any Luhansk village remains under Ukrainian control in late 2026 is uncertain.
war-2025-2026.military: Fighting on the Luhansk-Kharkiv-Donetsk junction around Borova and Lyman continued in 2026, including Ukraine's Operation Vivaldi on the Lyman front (May-October 2026); Ukrainian drones and missiles struck military targets deep in occupied Luhansk.

links.title: Ukraine says Bilohorivka mostly lost (Ukrainska Pravda, July 2025)

sources.title: Ukrainian forces liberate Nadiia (Euromaidan Press, March 2025)

UA-14.name: Donetsk Oblast
UA-14.overview: Today's Donetsk Oblast stretches from the Siverskyi Donets to the Sea of Azov. Its steppe was home to Neolithic cemeteries near Mariupol, Bronze Age herders, Scythians, Sarmatians and a long series of nomads, and it saw the Rus'-Cuman defeat by the Mongols on the Kalka in 1223. From the 17th century Cossacks, salt-workers, Greek, Serbian and German colonists settled it, and after John Hughes founded Yuzovka (Donetsk) in 1869 it became the heart of the Donbas coal and steel economy. Russian-backed forces seized Donetsk city and much of the south-east in 2014, and since 2022 most of the oblast has been the main battlefield of Russia's full-scale war, with Mariupol, Bakhmut, Avdiivka and Pokrovsk destroyed or captured and the Kramatorsk-Sloviansk area still held by Ukraine in late 2026.

trypillia.summary: Trypillian farmers did not reach this area. Near Mariupol a large Neolithic cemetery gave its name to the Mariupol culture of the Dnieper-Donets horizon, and Sredny Stog-type herders appeared later.

bronze-age-steppe.summary: The steppe was covered with Yamnaya and Catacomb kurgans; later Srubna-culture people mined copper on the Donets Ridge around Bakhmut and smelted it locally.

cimmerians.control: Early Iron Age nomads (Bilozerka and Cimmerian-period cultures)
cimmerians.summary: Late Bronze Age Bilozerka-type communities gave way to mobile nomads associated with the Cimmerians.

scythians.summary: The Azov steppe was Scythian pasture; Greek traders from the Bosporan cities reached the coast. Persian king Darius I's campaign of about 513 BCE may have crossed these steppes.

sarmatians.summary: Sarmatian tribes held the steppe and traded with Tanais at the mouth of the Don and the Bosporan Kingdom.

goths-chernyakhov.control: Alans and Sarmatians; Gothic raiders on the Azov coast
goths-chernyakhov.summary: Alans dominated the steppe while Goths launched sea raids from the Azov coast in the 250s-260s CE.

huns.summary: The Huns subdued the Alans of the area around 370 and moved on westwards.

antes.summary: Bulgar groups ranged over the Azov steppe; in the 630s it was part of Kubrat's Old Great Bulgaria.

east-slavic-tribes.summary: The hillfort and cemetery at Mayaky near Sloviansk is one of the two type sites of the Saltovo-Mayaki culture, which spread along the Donets under Khazar rule.
east-slavic-tribes.military: The Mayaky white-stone fortress guarded the Donets crossing.

kyivan-rus-formation.summary: Pechenegs moved into the steppe in the 10th century; Khazar-era settlements were abandoned after 965.

kyivan-rus-volodymyr.summary: The area remained Pecheneg pasture, beyond the reach of Kyiv.

kyivan-rus-peak.summary: Torks displaced the Pechenegs and were themselves driven out by the Cumans around 1060.

rus-fragmentation.summary: The Donets steppe was a centre of the Donets Cumans, whose stone statues survive in many local museums. Igor Sviatoslavich's defeat on the Kayala in 1185 may have happened here, but the location is disputed.
rus-fragmentation.military: Rus' princes campaigned into the Cuman steppe in 1111 and 1185.

galicia-volhynia.control: Cuman steppe, conquered by the Mongols
galicia-volhynia.summary: On 31 May 1223 the Mongols routed a Rus'-Cuman army on the Kalka river, usually identified with the Kalchyk near Mariupol, the first Mongol victory over the Rus'. The steppe fell to the Mongols in 1237-1240.
galicia-volhynia.military: The Battle of the Kalka River killed several Rus' princes, including Mstislav of Kyiv.

mongol-period.summary: The Azov steppe was Golden Horde pasture with little settled life.

lithuania-poland.control: Wild Fields; Crimean Tatar and Nogai pasture
lithuania-poland.summary: The steppe was crossed by the Kalmius Trail, a Tatar raiding route. The Sviatohirsk cave monastery on the Donets is first mentioned in 1526.

commonwealth.control: Wild Fields; Muscovite and Cossack frontier
commonwealth.summary: Zaporozhian and Don Cossacks boiled salt at the Tor lakes (today's Sloviansk) and fished the Azov rivers; Muscovite guard posts watched the Donets.
commonwealth.military: Muscovy founded the fortress of Tor at the salt lakes in 1645.

cossack-hetmanate.control: Muscovite frontier; Zaporozhian lands in the south-west
cossack-hetmanate.summary: Tor grew as a salt-making settlement, and Ukrainian settlers began to arrive in the north. The southern steppe was Zaporozhian hunting ground and Nogai pasture.

the-ruin.control: Muscovy (Izium regiment lands); Zaporozhian and Don Cossack zones
the-ruin.summary: Bakhmut was founded as a salt-works settlement in the 1680s. A conflict over the Bakhmut salt works between the Izium regiment and the Don Cossacks led to Kondraty Bulavin's rebellion of 1707-1708.
the-ruin.military: Bulavin's Cossacks seized the Bakhmut salt works and launched a rising against Peter I that was crushed in 1708.

hetmanate-decline.control: Russian Empire (Bakhmut province, Slavo-Serbia); Zaporozhian Kalmius palanka
hetmanate-decline.summary: The southern area belonged to the Kalmius palanka of the Zaporozhian Host, with a Cossack post at the site of later Mariupol. Bakhmut became a fortress town and in 1753 the north-east was settled as part of Slavo-Serbia.
hetmanate-decline.military: Bakhmut fortress and Slavo-Serbian hussar regiments guarded the frontier against the Crimean Khanate.

partitions-crimea.summary: After the Zaporozhian Sich was destroyed in 1775, Orthodox Greeks moved from Crimea in 1778-1780 founded Mariupol and some 20 villages on the Azov coast.

two-empires.control: Russian Empire (Yekaterinoslav Governorate: Bakhmut and Mariupol districts)
two-empires.summary: Ukrainian and Russian peasants, German and Mennonite colonists and Greek villages filled the steppe. Coal was mined on a small scale and Mariupol developed as a grain-exporting port.

national-revival.summary: In 1869 the Welsh industrialist John Hughes founded the New Russia Company ironworks and the town of Yuzovka, today's Donetsk. The Donbas became the empire's main coal and steel region, with railways, Mariupol's steelworks of the 1890s and a multiethnic workforce, and saw large strikes in 1905.

ukrainian-revolution.control: Contested: Bolsheviks, UNR and Hetmanate with German forces
ukrainian-revolution.summary: In 1918 the Bolsheviks included the area in the short-lived Donetsk-Krivoy Rog Soviet Republic; German, Austro-Hungarian and UNR troops drove them out in April 1918.
ukrainian-revolution.military: Red Guard detachments from the mines fought the advancing German and Ukrainian forces in spring 1918.

soviet-takeover.control: Contested by Whites, Makhnovists and Reds; Soviet from 1920
soviet-takeover.summary: Denikin's forces held the Donbas for much of 1919, while Nestor Makhno's insurgents operated in the south around Mariupol. Under Soviet rule the area formed the Donets Governorate with its capital in Bakhmut.
soviet-takeover.military: Makhno's insurgent army fought both the Whites and, later, the Red Army across the Azov steppe.

soviet-ukraine-1920s.summary: Yuzovka was renamed Stalino in 1924 and Bakhmut became Artemivsk. Industrialization brought rapid growth of mines and plants.

holodomor-terror.control: Ukrainian SSR (Donetsk Oblast from 1932, Stalino Oblast from 1938)
holodomor-terror.summary: Rural districts suffered heavily in the Holodomor while industrial towns grew. In 1937-1938 the NKVD's Greek Operation arrested and shot thousands of Azov Greeks.

soviet-annexations.summary: The Stalino region was the USSR's main coal basin and a centre of steel production at Mariupol, Makiivka and Kramatorsk.

nazi-occupation.summary: German forces occupied the area in October 1941. About 8,000 Jews were shot near Mariupol in October 1941 and thousands of residents were sent to Germany as forced labourers.
nazi-occupation.military: The Soviet Donbas offensive of August-September 1943 liberated the region; Stalino was freed on 8 September 1943 and Mariupol on 10 September.

postwar-ussr.summary: Mines and steelworks were rebuilt, partly by prisoners of war; Mariupol was renamed Zhdanov in 1948. Large-scale migration from Russia increased the Russian-speaking population.

soviet-ukraine-late.summary: Stalino became Donetsk in 1961 and was heavily Russified. The poet Vasyl Stus, who grew up in Donetsk, became one of Ukraine's best-known dissidents. In 1989 Donbas miners joined the Soviet-wide strikes.

independence.summary: About 77% of voters backed independence in 1991. Mine closures, strikes in 1993 and the rise of regional business clans around Rinat Akhmetov marked the 1990s; Viktor Yanukovych was governor in 1997-2002.

orange-to-euromaidan.summary: Donetsk was the base of the Party of Regions and of Yanukovych, president from 2010. The city hosted Euro 2012 matches at the Donbas Arena.

crimea-donbas-war.control: Split: Russian-backed 'Donetsk People's Republic' in the south-east, Ukraine in the north and west
crimea-donbas-war.summary: Separatists proclaimed the 'Donetsk People's Republic' on 7 April 2014, and a Russian-led armed group under Igor Girkin seized Sloviansk until 5 July 2014. Russian forces intervened openly at Ilovaisk in August 2014; Malaysia Airlines Flight MH17 was shot down over the oblast on 17 July 2014. Kramatorsk became the Ukrainian regional centre, and a front line near Avdiivka, Marinka and Horlivka persisted until 2022.
crimea-donbas-war.military: Key battles included Sloviansk (April-July 2014), Ilovaisk (August 2014), Donetsk Airport (2014-2015) and Debaltseve (January-February 2015); the Azov and Donbas volunteer battalions defended Mariupol and the coast.

full-scale-invasion.control: Contested: south and south-east occupied, north-west held by Ukraine
full-scale-invasion.summary: Russian forces besieged Mariupol from late February until the Azovstal garrison surrendered on 20 May 2022; the city was largely destroyed and the drama theatre bombing of 16 March killed hundreds. A missile strike on Kramatorsk station killed 61 evacuees in April, and about 50 Ukrainian prisoners died in the Olenivka prison explosion in July. Russia claimed to annex the oblast in September 2022.
full-scale-invasion.military: Volnovakha and Lyman were lost in spring 2022, Lyman was retaken on 1 October, and the Battle of Bakhmut began in August 2022; Russian assaults on Vuhledar failed with heavy losses in early 2023.

war-of-attrition.control: Contested: Russia gradually expanding its occupation westward
war-of-attrition.summary: Russia captured Bakhmut in May 2023 after the war's longest battle, Marinka in late 2023, Avdiivka in February 2024 and Vuhledar in October 2024, then advanced towards Pokrovsk from mid-2024 and took Kurakhove around the turn of 2025. Towns along the front were largely destroyed.
war-of-attrition.military: Wagner Group and regular Russian forces led the Bakhmut assault; Ukraine's brief 2023 counteroffensive retook villages near Bakhmut and Staromaiorske; fighting for Chasiv Yar and Toretsk began in 2024.

war-2025-2026.control: Mostly Russian-occupied (roughly three-quarters or more); Ukraine holds the Sloviansk-Kramatorsk-Druzhkivka belt; Kostiantynivka contested
war-2025-2026.summary: Russia took Toretsk and Chasiv Yar in 2025, broke into Pokrovsk in November 2025 and claimed it on 1 December; Pokrovsk and Myrnohrad were reported captured by early 2026. Russia also claimed Siversk in December 2025. The Battle of Kostiantynivka began in October 2025; Russia claimed the city in July 2026, but ISW still assessed it as contested. Russia demanded the rest of the oblast in peace talks, which Ukraine rejected.
war-2025-2026.military: A Russian breakthrough near Dobropillia in August 2025 was contained; Lyman came under renewed assault from mid-2026, while Ukraine's Operation Vivaldi on the Lyman front (May-October 2026) claimed about 277 km² recovered. Kramatorsk, Sloviansk and Druzhkivka remain Ukrainian-held under drone and glide-bomb attack; exact lines around Kostiantynivka, Siversk and Lyman are uncertain.

links.title: Kostiantynivka: both sides' claims wrong (Meduza, July 2026)

Ukrainska Pravda: situation in Donetsk Oblast (Nov 2025)

UA-12.name: Dnipropetrovsk Oblast
UA-12.overview: Centred on the great bend and former rapids of the Dnieper, today's Dnipropetrovsk Oblast has Neolithic cemeteries, Bronze Age kurgans and some of the richest Scythian royal burials, including Tovsta Mohyla and Chortomlyk. After centuries as nomad steppe it became the heartland of the Zaporozhian Cossacks, whose Siches at Tomakivka, Bazavluk, Mykytyn Rih, Chortomlyk and Pokrovske lay here, and Khmelnytsky's 1648 uprising began with victory at Zhovti Vody. Yekaterinoslav (Dnipro), founded under Catherine II, grew with Kryvyi Rih iron ore into a major industrial and later Soviet rocket-building centre that produced leaders from Brezhnev to Kuchma. Since 2014 it has been a key rear base of Ukraine's war effort; in 2025 Russian troops entered its eastern edge, and a Ukrainian counteroffensive in 2026 retook most of that ground.

trypillia.control: Neolithic-Eneolithic fishers, hunters and early herders
trypillia.summary: Along the Dnieper rapids, communities of the Dnieper-Donets culture left large collective cemeteries such as those at Vovnihy and Ihren near Dnipro. In the Eneolithic, Sredny Stog-type herders spread here; Trypillian farmers lived only to the west.

bronze-age-steppe.control: Yamnaya, Catacomb, Srubna and Sabatynivka pastoralists
bronze-age-steppe.summary: Yamnaya and Catacomb kurgans line the river terraces; in the Late Bronze Age the Dnieper valley belonged to the Sabatynivka culture, part of the Noua-Sabatinovka complex.

cimmerians.summary: Final Bronze Age Bilozerka settlements were replaced by mobile herders of the early Iron Age.

scythians.summary: The lower Dnieper around today's Nikopol and Pokrov was the burial land of the Scythian kings, often linked with Herodotus's Gerrhos. Its great kurgans include Chortomlyk and Tovsta Mohyla, where the famous gold pectoral was found in 1971.
scythians.military: Scythian elite burials held weapons, armour and horses of the royal cavalry.

sarmatians.summary: Sarmatians took the steppe from the Scythians, whose remaining state shrank to Crimea and the lower Dnieper below the rapids.

goths-chernyakhov.summary: Chernyakhov-culture farming villages stood along the Dnieper and its tributaries, part of the Gothic-led world the Goths called Oium.

huns.summary: The Hunnic conquest destroyed the Chernyakhov villages and turned the area back into nomad steppe.

antes.control: Antes (Penkovka culture) on the Dnieper; Bulgar and Avar nomads
antes.summary: Penkovka-culture settlements associated with the Antes reached down the Dnieper, while Kutrigur Bulgars and Avars held the open steppe.

east-slavic-tribes.control: Khazar steppe; Ulichians on the lower Dnieper; Magyars in passage
east-slavic-tribes.summary: The Slavic Ulichians lived along the lower Dnieper before moving west, and the Magyars passed through in the 9th century. The Dnieper rapids became a key stretch of the trade route from the Varangians to the Greeks.

kyivan-rus-formation.summary: Rus' merchants hauled their boats around the rapids, as described by Emperor Constantine VII around 950, while Pechenegs lay in wait. Prince Sviatoslav was killed by Pechenegs near the rapids in 972.
kyivan-rus-formation.military: Pecheneg ambushes at the rapids threatened every Rus' convoy.

links.title: Trade route from the Varangians to the Greeks

kyivan-rus-volodymyr.summary: The area lay south of Volodymyr's fortified lines; the river route remained Rus' lifeline to Byzantium.

kyivan-rus-peak.summary: After Yaroslav's victory over the Pechenegs in 1036 they were replaced by Torks and soon by Cumans.

rus-fragmentation.summary: The Dnieper Cumans controlled the steppe around the bend of the river, and the Samara river valley was a meeting zone between Cumans and Rus' traders.
rus-fragmentation.military: Rus' princes repeatedly campaigned down the Dnieper against the Cumans, as in 1103 and 1111.

galicia-volhynia.control: Cuman steppe, conquered by the Mongols
galicia-volhynia.summary: Rus' armies marched through on their way to the Kalka in 1223; the Mongols took the area during their 1239-1240 campaigns.

mongol-period.summary: The area was Golden Horde pasture; a Horde town flourished at Kamianka on the Dnieper nearby.

lithuania-poland.control: Wild Fields; Lithuanian then Polish claims, Crimean Tatar raiding zone
lithuania-poland.summary: Cossacks, fishermen and hunters from the Kyiv region began to camp beyond the rapids. By the 1560s the Zaporozhian Host had its Sich on Tomakivka island near today's Marhanets.
lithuania-poland.military: Tomakivka Sich (c. 1564-1593) was the stronghold of the Zaporozhian Cossacks; it was destroyed by the Tatars in 1593.

commonwealth.control: Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth claims; Zaporozhian Cossack self-rule
commonwealth.summary: The Sich moved to Bazavluk (1593-1638) and then Mykytyn Rih at today's Nikopol (1639-1652). To control the Cossacks, Poland built Kodak fortress above the rapids in 1635; Ivan Sulyma's Cossacks destroyed it the same year, and it was rebuilt in 1639.
commonwealth.military: Kodak fortress, the Bazavluk and Mykytyn Siches and Cossack sea campaigns against the Ottomans defined the area.

cossack-hetmanate.control: Zaporozhian Host (allied to the Cossack Hetmanate)
cossack-hetmanate.summary: Bohdan Khmelnytsky launched his uprising from the Mykytyn Sich in early 1648 and won his first victory at Zhovti Vody in May 1648. In 1652 the Sich moved to Chortomlyk.
cossack-hetmanate.military: The Battle of Zhovti Vody (April-May 1648) destroyed the Polish vanguard; the Cossacks also took Kodak fortress.

the-ruin.summary: Chortomlyk Sich (1652-1709) near today's Kapulivka was the Zaporozhian capital, and its koshovyi otaman Ivan Sirko led famous raids on Crimea; he is buried at Kapulivka.
the-ruin.military: Sirko's Zaporozhians raided the Crimean Khanate and Ottoman fortresses on the lower Dnieper.

hetmanate-decline.control: Zaporozhian Host under Russian suzerainty (Nova Sich); Crimean influence until 1734
hetmanate-decline.summary: After the Zaporozhians backed Mazepa, Russian troops destroyed Chortomlyk Sich in 1709. The Cossacks returned in 1734 and founded the New (Pidpilna) Sich near today's Pokrov, ruling a territory of palankas with growing farming settlements such as Samara (Novomoskovsk).
hetmanate-decline.military: The Zaporozhians fought for Russia in the Russo-Turkish wars of 1735-1739 and 1768-1774.

partitions-crimea.summary: In June 1775 Russian troops destroyed the New Sich and exiled its last otaman, Petro Kalnyshevsky. Yekaterinoslav was founded on the Dnieper in 1776/1787 under Grigory Potemkin, and the land was handed out to nobles and colonists. The wooden Trinity Cathedral at Novomoskovsk, built by Zaporozhian craftsmen, dates from 1775-1781.

two-empires.summary: Yekaterinoslav was a modest provincial capital with a large Jewish community; the steppe was settled by Ukrainian serfs, state peasants and German and Jewish agricultural colonies.

national-revival.summary: The Catherine Railway (1884) linked Kryvyi Rih iron ore with Donbas coal, and Yekaterinoslav and Kamianske boomed with steelworks. The historian Dmytro Yavornytsky collected Zaporozhian heritage and led the city's history museum.

ukrainian-revolution.control: Contested: UNR, Bolsheviks, Hetmanate with German and Austrian troops
ukrainian-revolution.summary: Yekaterinoslav changed hands repeatedly between the Central Rada, Bolsheviks and the Hetmanate. In December 1918 Nestor Makhno's insurgents briefly seized the city.
ukrainian-revolution.military: Makhnovist, UNR and Bolshevik forces fought for the city and the railway junctions.

soviet-takeover.control: Contested by Whites, Makhnovists and Reds; Soviet from 1920
soviet-takeover.summary: Denikin's forces took Yekaterinoslav in mid-1919, Makhno held it in late 1919, and the Bolsheviks secured the region in 1920; Wrangel's troops fought near Nikopol that year.
soviet-takeover.military: Makhno's Revolutionary Insurgent Army held Yekaterinoslav for about a month in November-December 1919.

soviet-ukraine-1920s.summary: Yekaterinoslav was renamed Dnipropetrovsk in 1926. The building of the DniproHES dam downstream (1927-1932) flooded the rapids and powered new industry in the region.

holodomor-terror.summary: The newly created oblast was among the worst hit by the Holodomor. The Kryvorizhstal steel plant began production in 1934 and the purges hit local party and factory managers.

soviet-annexations.summary: The region was a core of Soviet metallurgy; Leonid Brezhnev, a native of Kamianske, rose in the Dnipropetrovsk party apparatus.

nazi-occupation.summary: Dnipropetrovsk fell on 25 August 1941, and about 11,000 Jews were murdered there in October 1941. The city was liberated on 25 October 1943; Nikopol and Kryvyi Rih followed in February 1944.
nazi-occupation.military: The Battle of the Dnieper (autumn 1943) and the Nikopol-Kryvyi Rih offensive (early 1944) were fought across the oblast.

postwar-ussr.summary: A car plant in Dnipropetrovsk was converted in 1951 into the Pivdenmash (Yuzhmash) missile factory, and the city was closed to foreigners.
postwar-ussr.military: Pivdenmash began series production of ballistic missiles in the early 1950s.

soviet-ukraine-late.summary: Mikhail Yangel's Pivdenne design bureau (from 1954) and Pivdenmash built ICBMs such as the R-36 and space rockets, and Brezhnev's 'Dnipropetrovsk clan' dominated Soviet leadership. Leonid Kuchma was Pivdenmash's director in 1986-1992.
soviet-ukraine-late.military: Dnipropetrovsk was a closed city producing strategic missiles for the Soviet Strategic Rocket Forces.

independence.summary: Dnipropetrovsk politicians dominated the 1990s: Leonid Kuchma was president in 1994-2005, and Pavlo Lazarenko and Yulia Tymoshenko built business empires in gas trading. The PrivatBank group was founded in the city.

orange-to-euromaidan.summary: Yulia Tymoshenko, from Dnipropetrovsk, became prime minister after the Orange Revolution. The 2004 sale of Kryvorizhstal was annulled and the plant was resold to Mittal Steel in 2005.

crimea-donbas-war.control: Ukraine (rear base of the Donbas front)
crimea-donbas-war.summary: Governor Ihor Kolomoisky's administration suppressed separatist mobilisation in 2014 and funded volunteer units. Dnipro became the main hospital, logistics and volunteer hub for the front, and the city was renamed Dnipro in 2016. Volodymyr Zelensky, from Kryvyi Rih, was elected president in 2019.
crimea-donbas-war.military: Volunteer battalions such as Dnipro-1 were raised here, and the Mechnikov hospital treated thousands of wounded soldiers.

full-scale-invasion.control: Ukraine (not occupied; under missile and artillery attack)
full-scale-invasion.summary: The oblast was not occupied in 2022 but became a rear hub for the eastern and southern fronts. Nikopol and Marhanets were shelled almost daily from Russian-held Enerhodar across the Kakhovka reservoir, and a Russian missile hit an apartment block in Dnipro on 14 January 2023, killing 46 people.
full-scale-invasion.military: Units staged through the oblast for the Kherson and Donbas fronts; Kryvyi Rih's southern approaches were close to the Kherson front until November 2022.

war-of-attrition.summary: The destruction of the Kakhovka dam in June 2023 drained the reservoir, cutting water supplies to Nikopol, Marhanets and Kryvyi Rih areas. Missile and drone attacks on Dnipro and Kryvyi Rih continued, and by late 2024 Russian advances near Pokrovsk and Kurakhove approached the oblast's eastern border.
war-of-attrition.military: Nikopol district remained under constant drone and artillery fire from across the drained reservoir.

war-2025-2026.control: Ukraine; small eastern border areas briefly occupied in 2025, mostly retaken in 2026
war-2025-2026.summary: A Russian missile strike on Kryvyi Rih on 4 April 2025 killed 20 people, including 9 children. From mid-2025 Russian troops crossed into the oblast's eastern edge near Mezhova and Pokrovske hromadas and occupied a number of villages. Ukraine's counteroffensive from 11 February 2026 on the Dnipropetrovsk-Zaporizhzhia border retook most of this ground; by August 2026 Russia reportedly fully held only one village, Dachne, though such figures are uncertain.
war-2025-2026.military: Ukraine claimed about 745 km² and 26 settlements recaptured by August 2026 across the Dnipropetrovsk, Zaporizhzhia and Donetsk border zone; fighting around Ternove, Berezove and Voskresenka shifted back and forth, and Nikopol and the eastern hromadas remain under daily attack.

UA-23.name: Zaporizhzhia Oblast
UA-23.overview: Today's Zaporizhzhia Oblast runs from the former Dnieper rapids and Khortytsia island south to the Sea of Azov. Its steppe holds the prehistoric rock art of Kamiana Mohyla, Scythian royal kurgans such as Solokha and the great Kamianka hillfort, and it was crossed by nomads from Sarmatians to Cumans; Rus' princes gathered at Khortytsia before the Kalka battle in 1223. In the 16th-18th centuries Khortytsia was the cradle of the Zaporozhian Cossacks, while the south was Nogai pasture; after 1775 the area was colonised by Ukrainians, Russians, Mennonites, Bulgarians and others, and Huliaipole became the home of Nestor Makhno's anarchist movement. Soviet industrialization built the DniproHES dam and later Europe's largest nuclear plant at Enerhodar; since 2022 Russia has occupied the south, including Melitopol, Berdiansk and the nuclear plant, while Zaporizhzhia city remains Ukrainian close to the front.

trypillia.summary: The Sredny Stog culture is named after Seredni Stih island on the Dnieper near Zaporizhzhia. The sandstone hill of Kamiana Mohyla near Melitopol bears thousands of carvings from the Stone Age onwards.

bronze-age-steppe.summary: Yamnaya and Catacomb herders built thousands of kurgans across the Azov steppe and left carvings at Kamiana Mohyla. Later Srubna and Sabatynivka groups settled along the Dnieper and Molochna.

cimmerians.summary: Final Bronze Age Bilozerka communities lived along the Dnieper, followed by early Iron Age nomads linked with the Cimmerians.

scythians.summary: The left bank of the lower Dnieper was a core of Scythia: the Solokha kurgan yielded a famous gold comb, and the Melitopol kurgan and others held royal burials. The vast Kamianka hillfort near Kamianka-Dniprovska was a Scythian metalworking centre and possibly a capital in the 5th-3rd centuries BCE.
scythians.military: The Kamianka hillfort was fortified with earth ramparts and the Dnieper floodplain; Scythian elite burials contain rich weapons and horse gear.

sarmatians.summary: Sarmatians overran the Azov steppe, while the reduced Late Scythian state held settlements on the lower Dnieper and in Crimea.

goths-chernyakhov.control: Chernyakhov culture on the Dnieper; Alans on the steppe
goths-chernyakhov.summary: Chernyakhov villages stood on the Dnieper terraces, while Alans and Goths controlled the Azov steppe.

huns.summary: The Huns swept across the Azov steppe in the 370s, ending the Gothic-Alan order.

antes.summary: Bulgar groups and then the Avars held the steppe; Antes lived further up the Dnieper.

east-slavic-tribes.summary: A rich late 7th- or early 8th-century complex with silver and weapons, found at Voznesenka (today in Zaporizhzhia city), is linked with a Bulgar or Khazar ruler. Khazars dominated the steppe.

kyivan-rus-formation.control: Pecheneg steppe; Rus' river route at Khortytsia
kyivan-rus-formation.summary: Constantine VII described Rus' traders resting at St Gregory's island (Khortytsia) after passing the rapids. Sviatoslav was killed by the Pecheneg khan Kurya near the rapids in 972.
kyivan-rus-formation.military: The Khortytsia crossing (Kichkas ford) was a favourite Pecheneg ambush point.

kyivan-rus-volodymyr.summary: The Pechenegs dominated the region, and Rus' convoys to Byzantium passed only under armed escort.

kyivan-rus-peak.summary: Torks replaced the Pechenegs on the Azov steppe in the mid-11th century.

rus-fragmentation.summary: The Cumans controlled the steppe; Rus' traders used the Protolche ford near Khortytsia.
rus-fragmentation.military: Rus' coalitions marched down the Dnieper against the Cumans in 1103 and later campaigns.

galicia-volhynia.control: Cuman steppe, conquered by the Mongols
galicia-volhynia.summary: In spring 1223 the Rus' princes, including Mstislav of Galicia, assembled with the Cumans at Khortytsia and the Protolche ford before marching to the Kalka, where they were defeated. The Mongols took the area in 1239-1240.
galicia-volhynia.military: The Rus'-Cuman army of 1223 crossed the Dnieper near Khortytsia.

mongol-period.summary: A Golden Horde town at Kamianka-Dniprovska and nomad camps on the Molochna marked the area.

lithuania-poland.control: Wild Fields; Crimean Khanate and Nogai pasture; Cossack outposts
lithuania-poland.summary: In the 1550s Prince Dmytro Vyshnevetsky built a fortress on Mala Khortytsia, seen as a forerunner of the Zaporozhian Sich. The southern steppe belonged to Nogai nomads subject to the Crimean Khan.
lithuania-poland.military: Vyshnevetsky's Khortytsia castle withstood a Crimean siege in 1557 before being abandoned.

commonwealth.control: Zaporozhian Cossack lands (north); Nogai and Crimean Tatar steppe (south)
commonwealth.summary: Zaporozhian Cossacks camped, fished and hunted around Khortytsia and the Velykyi Luh floodplain, while the Nogai roamed the Molochna and Azov coast.
commonwealth.military: The Velykyi Luh floodplain sheltered Cossack bands and boats for raids on Crimea and the Ottoman coast.

cossack-hetmanate.control: Zaporozhian Host lands (north); Crimean Khanate's Nogai lands (south)
cossack-hetmanate.summary: The northern part of the oblast was Zaporozhian territory around the Sich, while Nogai hordes held the south as allies of the Crimean Khan, who sometimes fought alongside Khmelnytsky.

the-ruin.summary: Zaporozhian winter homesteads (zymivnyky) spread along the Dnieper tributaries, while Nogai raids crossed the steppe.
the-ruin.military: Ivan Sirko's Cossacks fought Tatar and Nogai forces on the Molochna steppe.

hetmanate-decline.control: Zaporozhian Host under Russian suzerainty (north); Crimean Khanate (south) until 1770s
hetmanate-decline.summary: The north belonged to the Kodak and other palankas of the New Sich. During the Russo-Turkish war of 1768-1774 Russia built the Dnieper Line, including Oleksandrivsk fortress (1770), the origin of Zaporizhzhia city.
hetmanate-decline.military: The Dnieper Line of forts from the Dnieper to the Azov coast pushed Russia's frontier towards Crimea.

partitions-crimea.summary: The Sich was destroyed in 1775 and Crimea annexed in 1783, after which most Nogai were removed. In 1789 Mennonites from Prussia founded the Chortitza colony at Khortytsia.

two-empires.summary: The Molochna Mennonite colony (from 1804), Bulgarian, German, Doukhobor and Nogai villages and Ukrainian and Russian peasants filled the steppe. Berdiansk (1827) and Melitopol grew as grain towns and ports.

national-revival.summary: Railways linked Oleksandrivsk and Melitopol to ports and markets, and Mennonite firms made the area a centre of farm machinery production. Nestor Makhno was born in Huliaipole in 1888.

ukrainian-revolution.control: Contested: UNR and Hetmanate with Austro-German troops; Makhnovist anarchists
ukrainian-revolution.summary: Makhno organised an anarchist movement in Huliaipole from 1917 and led guerrilla war against Austro-German forces and the Hetmanate in 1918.
ukrainian-revolution.military: Makhno's insurgents defeated Austro-Hungarian and Hetmanate units at Dibrivka in September 1918.

soviet-takeover.control: Contested by Makhnovists, Whites and Reds; Soviet from late 1920
soviet-takeover.summary: The Huliaipole region formed the heart of Makhno's Free Territory. In 1920 Wrangel's White army advanced into Northern Taurida, and after Wrangel's defeat the Red Army turned on Makhno's army in November 1920.
soviet-takeover.military: Makhno's Revolutionary Insurgent Army, Wrangel's Russian Army and the Red Army fought across the area in 1919-1920.

soviet-ukraine-1920s.summary: Oleksandrivsk was renamed Zaporizhzhia in 1921. The DniproHES dam and power station (1927-1932) flooded the rapids and anchored a new industrial city; many Mennonites emigrated.

holodomor-terror.summary: Ukrainian, Mennonite and other villages suffered the Holodomor and deportations; Zaporizhstal and aluminium plants opened in the 1930s. Mennonite and German men were heavily targeted in the Great Terror.

soviet-annexations.summary: Zaporizhzhia Oblast was created in January 1939. The Zaporizhzhia industrial complex was one of the USSR's largest steel and aluminium centres.

nazi-occupation.summary: Soviet troops blew up the DniproHES dam in August 1941, and the factories were evacuated east before Zaporizhzhia fell in early October 1941. Many ethnic Germans were deported east by the Soviets before the occupation.
nazi-occupation.military: The Red Army liberated Zaporizhzhia on 14 October 1943 and Melitopol on 23 October after breaking the German Wotan line; the Nikopol bridgehead on the left bank held until February 1944.

postwar-ussr.summary: DniproHES was rebuilt by 1950 and Zaporizhstal resumed steel production; the city grew rapidly as an industrial centre.

soviet-ukraine-late.summary: The Kakhovka reservoir (1956) drowned the Velykyi Luh floodplain, the ZAZ plant built Zaporozhets cars from 1960, and the Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant was built at Enerhodar from 1980.
soviet-ukraine-late.military: Motor Sich in Zaporizhzhia built aircraft and helicopter engines for the Soviet armed forces.

independence.summary: The sixth reactor at Enerhodar (1995) made the plant the largest in Europe, and Khortytsia became a national reserve dedicated to Cossack history in 1993. Motor Sich remained a major aero-engine producer.

orange-to-euromaidan.summary: The Party of Regions dominated the south of the oblast; in January 2014 Euromaidan protesters in Zaporizhzhia were dispersed from the regional administration.

crimea-donbas-war.control: Ukraine (rear area near the Donbas and Crimea fronts)
crimea-donbas-war.summary: Separatist activity in Zaporizhzhia and Melitopol was contained in 2014. The Azov volunteer battalion was formed in Berdiansk in May 2014, and Russia's control of the Kerch Strait from 2018 squeezed the Azov port of Berdiansk.
crimea-donbas-war.military: The Azov unit was raised in Berdiansk and moved to the Mariupol front; Zaporizhzhia became a training and repair base for the army.

full-scale-invasion.control: Split: south (about 70%) occupied by Russia; Zaporizhzhia city and north held by Ukraine
full-scale-invasion.summary: Russian forces from Crimea took Berdiansk and Melitopol in late February and early March 2022 and seized Enerhodar and the nuclear plant on 4 March, raising international fears of a nuclear accident. Melitopol's mayor Ivan Fedorov was abducted, and partisans became active. Zaporizhzhia city received refugees from Mariupol; a missile strike on a civilian convoy there killed about 30 people on 30 September 2022, the day Russia claimed to annex the oblast.
full-scale-invasion.military: The front stabilised by spring 2022 roughly along Kamianske-Orikhiv-Huliaipole; Russian shelling of the nuclear plant area and Enerhodar battle (4 March 2022) drew IAEA missions.

war-of-attrition.control: Split: south occupied by Russia; north held by Ukraine
war-of-attrition.summary: Ukraine's June 2023 counteroffensive towards Tokmak and Melitopol stalled in minefields of the Surovikin line, gaining only Robotyne and a few nearby villages. The destruction of the Kakhovka dam in June 2023 drained the reservoir that cooled the nuclear plant, which stayed in cold shutdown under Russian control.
war-of-attrition.military: Heavy fighting around Robotyne, Verbove and Orikhiv in 2023 was followed by Russian pressure from 2024 that gradually pushed Ukraine back from the Robotyne salient.

war-2025-2026.control: Split: south and an expanding eastern zone occupied by Russia; Zaporizhzhia city, Orikhiv and the north held by Ukraine
war-2025-2026.summary: From late 2025 Russian forces pushed west from the Donetsk border, capturing Huliaipole (reported January 2026) and advancing towards Orikhiv, and also pressed at Stepnohirsk and Prymorske about 20 km south of Zaporizhzhia city after taking Kamianske in 2025. From February 2026 Ukrainian counterattacks on the Dnipropetrovsk-Zaporizhzhia border regained villages in the north-east. Zaporizhzhia city and the region suffered hundreds of drone, artillery and glide-bomb strikes per day, and the nuclear plant remained occupied and repeatedly lost off-site power.
war-2025-2026.military: The front in late 2026 ran roughly from the Dnieper near Stepnohirsk through Orikhiv to the Huliaipole area; the Huliaipole and Orikhiv sectors were the most active, and the exact line is uncertain.
